title: A closed subscheme whose fibres are quasi-regular immersions is locally contained in a relative quasi-regular immersion, and agrees with one under flatness or under the codimension count

standard_prerequisites.name: The relation between quasi-regularity and regularity of a sequence after localization, and the persistence of a regular sequence in a neighbourhood of a prime
standard_prerequisites.use: Turns the quasi-regular sequence generating the fibre ideal into a regular sequence on a neighbourhood, which is what the iterative construction needs.

standard_prerequisites.name: The fibrewise criterion for a closed subscheme to be a relative effective Cartier divisor, applied one equation at a time, cited from the same chapter
standard_prerequisites.use: Produces each successive member of the filtration by vanishing loci of the chosen sequence.

standard_prerequisites.name: A surjective map of flat local algebras essentially of finite presentation that becomes an isomorphism after dividing by the maximal ideal of the base is an isomorphism, and the local criterion for an isomorphism in a neighbourhood
standard_prerequisites.use: Upgrades the containment of part (1) to equality in the flat case of part (2).

standard_prerequisites.name: The dimension formula at a point of a finite type scheme over a field and the drop of dimension by one on cutting out a nonzerodivisor
standard_prerequisites.use: Shows that the number of equations cutting out the fibre in the hypothesis of part (3) equals the length of the regular sequence constructed in part (1).

core_obligations: Set up the local algebra as in the preceding fibrewise criterion, and use the hypothesis of (1) to shrink until the ideal of the closed subscheme in the fibre over the given base point is generated by a quasi-regular sequence, then localize so that chosen elements of the ideal map to that sequence and, by the cited regularity lemmas, form a regular sequence on the fibre (proof lines 5517-5536).

Construct the relative quasi-regular immersion by induction: applying the fibrewise Cartier criterion to the first equation produces a relative effective Cartier divisor, applying it again to the next equation inside that divisor produces another, and so on until the vanishing locus of the whole sequence is reached; that locus is then a regular immersion and flat over the base, hence a relative quasi-regular immersion (proof lines 5537-5548).

Prove part (2) by the isomorphism criterion: the surjection between the local rings of the two closed subschemes is a map of flat local algebras essentially of finite presentation which becomes an isomorphism modulo the maximal ideal of the base, so it is an isomorphism, and the local criterion upgrades this to an isomorphism on a neighbourhood (proof lines 5550-5560).

Prove part (3) by an equation count: after shrinking, the ideal of the constructed immersion is generated by a regular sequence of length r and the ideal of the given subscheme by c elements with c equal to the difference of the fibrewise dimensions; the dimension formula and the drop of dimension on cutting out a nonzerodivisor show r equals c, and since each equation of the first ideal is a combination of the equations of the second and the two cut out the same quasi-regular subscheme of the fibre, the transition matrix between the generating sequences is invertible modulo the maximal ideal and hence on a neighbourhood, so the two ideals agree there (proof lines 5562-5578).
Deduce the final statement from part (2) together with the equivalence between finite presentation over the base and over the ambient scheme (proof lines 5580-5594).
proof_roadmap: Reduce to affine rings, choose a quasi-regular sequence generating the fibre ideal, upgrade it to a regular sequence on a neighbourhood and build the required immersion one equation at a time by the fibrewise Cartier criterion (proof lines 5517-5548).

Get equality of the two closed subschemes in the flat case by the isomorphism criterion for flat local algebras, and in the equation-count case by comparing lengths through the dimension formula and showing the change-of-basis matrix is a unit near the point (proof lines 5550-5594).
difficulty_reason: The lemma is the quasi-regular counterpart of the fibrewise Cartier criterion: for a flat morphism locally of finite presentation and a closed subscheme whose fibre at a point is a quasi-regular immersion, it produces locally a relative quasi-regular immersion containing the subscheme and agreeing with it on the fibre, with equality under a flatness hypothesis or when the subscheme is cut out by the codimension number of equations, and it derives the corresponding global criterion (statement lines 5491-5515). The counted proof builds the required immersion as an iterated application of the fibrewise Cartier criterion along the chosen regular sequence, proving that each successive vanishing locus is a relative effective Cartier divisor in the previous one, and then compares the constructed immersion with the given subscheme either through the isomorphism criterion for flat local algebras or through the dimension formula and the invertibility of a change-of-basis matrix (proof lines 5517-5594). It is H2: the induction and both comparisons are carried out in the counted span, with the cited inputs being standard regularity and dimension facts.

This is the quasi-regular analogue of the lane's card S13-div-fibre-cartier (statement 4190-4213, proof 4215-4291), which is the fibrewise effective Cartier criterion and is cited inside this proof as an input; the two have different hypotheses and conclusions (quasi-regular immersions cut out by sequences versus single Cartier divisors) and their intervals are disjoint.

Assumption difference with S13-div-fibre-cartier: that card assumes the fibre is cut out by a single nonzerodivisor, this card assumes the fibre is a quasi-regular immersion cut out by a sequence (in part (3) by exactly the codimension number of equations). Conclusion difference: that card produces a relative effective Cartier divisor, this card produces a relative quasi-regular immersion, and the containment-to-equality arguments differ (the equation count r equals c is new here); this card uses that card rather than restating it.
